walkthroughs.body_html:
Economic Principles and Issues — a core area of A-Level Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Economic Principles and Issues brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Economic Principles and Issues.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: GDP per capita
GNI per capita
Population growth
Trade balance

mcqs.q: Sen argued development should be measured as:
options: GDP
Income
Capabilities
Employment

mcqs.q: How is economic growth shown on a Production Possibility Curve?
options: Both terms mean the same thing — government economic policy.
By an outward shift of the entire curve — reflecting an increase in productive capacity through more or better resources, technology, or skills.
Growth is shown by the curve becoming straighter.
Growth is shown by moving from inside the curve to a point on the curve.

mcqs.q: What did the original Phillips curve suggest, and how has thinking changed?
options: The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.
The Phillips curve still proves you can always reduce unemployment by allowing more inflation.

The original Phillips curve suggested a stable inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Friedman and the 1970s stagflation experience added expectations — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Both terms mean the same thing — government economic policy.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between monetary and fiscal policy?
options: Monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply controlled by the central bank; fiscal policy uses government taxation and spending controlled by the Treasury.
Monetary policy is about money and fiscal policy is about taxes.
The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.
Both terms mean the same thing — government economic policy.
